questions.question: Define drought properly, distinguish the four types in their order of deepening, and separate the natural causes from the human causes.
questions.expected_answer: A drought is an extended period of rainfall well below the normal average for that particular place — the definition must be anchored to the local average, since 250 millimetres is normal for Upington but catastrophic for Durban. The four types deepen in the order the water fails through the system: meteorological drought is the rainfall shortfall itself; agricultural drought follows when soil moisture drops below what crops and grazing need; hydrological drought arrives when the shortage reaches rivers, dams and groundwater; and socio-economic drought is reached when water supply can no longer meet human demand, driving prices, job losses and migration. Natural causes include southern Africa's position under the subtropical high-pressure belt, seasons when the ITCZ stalls short or the Kalahari High fails to weaken, El Niño years such as 2015-16 that reorganise the circulation toward dry summers, and climate change increasing evaporation and rainfall variability. Human causes deepen the natural shortfall: rising demand from growing populations and thirsty crops, leaking infrastructure, and degraded catchments that shed water instead of storing it.

questions.question: Explain what desertification is, the human chain of causes behind it, and why it operates as a self-feeding spiral, naming affected regions in Africa and South Africa.
questions.expected_answer: Desertification is the degradation of land in arid and semi-arid regions until it becomes desert-like — soil stripped of nutrients and vegetation, unable to hold water or support life. It is not a desert advancing but productive land dying in patches under human pressure. The causal chain runs: overgrazing strips grass faster than it regrows and compacts the soil; over-cultivation exhausts nutrients until soil crumbles to dust; deforestation for firewood leaves soil naked; and poor irrigation in hot climates causes salinisation as evaporating water leaves salt behind. Population pressure and poverty drive all four, and climate change multiplies them. The spiral is self-feeding because bare soil bakes hard, so rain runs off in flash floods that carve dongas and strip topsoil, wind lifts the loosened dust, and with less soil, less vegetation returns, exposing yet more ground to faster erosion. The Sahel along the southern edge of the Sahara is the world's warning region, while in South Africa the Karoo, the Kalahari margins and the crowded former homeland areas of the Eastern Cape show the classic gullies and dust.

questions.question: Using the Cape Town Day Zero crisis and named programmes, describe the effects of drought on people and the management strategies used against drought and desertification.
questions.expected_answer: Drought's human effects run from food security — the 2015-16 drought killed tens of thousands of cattle and forced South Africa to import maize as prices climbed — through lost farm livelihoods and drought migration to the cities, to health impacts and conflict over scarce water. Cape Town's Day Zero crisis followed three failed winter rainfall seasons from 2015 to 2017: dams fell toward 13 percent and the city published the date when taps would close and residents would queue for 25 litres each. The city cut demand by more than half, from around 1 200 million litres a day toward 500, using restrictions, steep tariffs, pressure management and a public campaign, and Day Zero never arrived. Management strategies group into three families. Seeing it coming: early warning from rainfall and El Niño monitoring with satellite images and GIS mapping of drought-prone districts, letting farmers destock early and plant drought-resistant crops. Using less: drip irrigation, night watering and mulching on farms, plus rainwater harvesting, greywater reuse, leak repair and tariffs in towns. Healing the land: rotational grazing and realistic stocking rates, crop rotation, contour ploughing, check dams in dongas, windbreaks, Working for Water clearing alien invasive plants to restore river flow while creating jobs, LandCare rehabilitation projects, and the Great Green Wall's community restoration mosaic across the Sahel.
